prime.problem: Some algorithms need a stride: a transpose must read rows and write columns, so one side is always uncoalesced and the naive kernel runs at 18% of a copy. You need somewhere on the chip to rearrange data cheaply, and that place has its own access rule that can serialise a warp 32 ways.
prime.fits: The coalescing card showed why the naive transpose's writes waste 7/8 of every sector. This card is the fix: stage the tile in shared memory. It introduces banks, __syncthreads() and padding, which the reduction cards and siboehm's kernel 3 reuse.
expect: shared memory as a per-block scratchpad
prime.goal: Explain each step of Harris's transpose ladder, compute which bank any tile element lands in, and pick a padding or swizzle that makes a column read conflict-free.

attend: Harris's copySharedMem runs as fast as copy. What two suspects does that one experiment rule out?
In transposeCoalesced, which thread wrote the element that a thread reads back from the tile, and why does that force a barrier?
Why does a column of float tile[32][32] land entirely in one bank, and what does one extra column change in the arithmetic?
Why does width 33 work but width 34 leave a 2-way conflict?
When would staging a copy through shared memory add nothing at all?

must: Transpose needs a stride on one side → read a 32 × 32 tile coalesced into shared memory → barrier → write it out coalesced from the mirrored position → the stride happens on-chip, where it costs no DRAM sectors
Threads read tile elements that other warps wrote → warps run in no fixed order → __syncthreads() is required between the store and the column read → every thread of the block must reach it
bank = word index mod 32 → a column of a 32-wide tile has word = 32i + j → every row maps to bank j → 32-way conflict → pad to 33 so bank = (i + j) mod 32 → one request serves the warp
Coalescing global memory gives the biggest step (2.73× on the M2050) → removing bank conflicts gives the rest (1.94×) → together 5.3×, about 95% of the fastest copy
elevated: Conflict degree for a float column read of a width-w tile is gcd(w, 32) → any odd width is conflict-free, 34 is 2-way, 48 is 16-way → an XOR swizzle reaches 1-way without extra bytes, which matters where padding would break 16-byte alignment for wide loads
reference: the M2050 and K20c GB/s table
per-GPU shared memory sizes (48 KB of 64 KB on Fermi, 64 KB on a T4, 228 KB on an H100) and the 48 KB dynamic opt-in

compress.prompt: Draw the transposeNoBankConflicts pipeline from memory: global row → tile → barrier → tile column → global row. Mark where each of the two problems (sectors, banks) would appear without the fix, and write the bank formula for a padded tile under it.
checklist: reads and writes of global memory are both along rows, so both coalesced
the column access happens in shared memory
the barrier is needed because a thread reads values another warp stored
bank = word mod 32; width 32 puts a column in one bank, width 33 spreads it across all 32
result: 18.8 → 51.3 → 99.5 GB/s on the M2050, ~95% of the fastest copy

retrieve.q: Explain why transposeCoalesced is still only about half of copy speed, even though every global access is now coalesced.
answer: the column read from tile[32][32] puts all 32 lanes in one bank
the hardware splits the request into 32 serial passes
so shared memory, not DRAM, is now the bottleneck: 51.3 GB/s on the M2050

retrieve.q: For float tile[32][33], compute the bank of tile[0][0], tile[1][0] and tile[31][0], and say how many requests a column read needs.
answer: all 32 rows land on different banks, so one request

retrieve.q: Pad or swizzle? Compare tile[32][33] with an XOR-swizzled tile[32][32]: what each costs, and where padding stops being the right answer.
answer: padding: one extra float per row (+128 B, +3.1%), trivial index math
swizzle: no extra bytes, but harder index math
padding breaks the 16-byte alignment that 128-bit loads and tensor-core loads (ldmatrix, TMA) need; there, swizzles win

retrieve.q: You remove __syncthreads() from transposeCoalesced and the output is right on your test. Why is the kernel still wrong, and which tool would catch it?
answer: a warp may read a column before the other 7 warps have stored their rows
passing a test only means the warps happened to run in a friendly order
Compute Sanitizer's racecheck flags the shared-memory read-after-write hazard

compare.q: The transpose tile and siboehm's kernel 3 tile both stage 32 × 32 floats in shared memory. What is each tile for, and why does one give 5.3× and the other only 1.5×?
answer: transpose: rearrange data so both global sides are coalesced; each value is used once
kernel 3: reuse each loaded value 32 times to cut global loads
the transpose's bottleneck was DRAM waste, which staging removes; kernel 3's bottleneck moved to two shared-memory loads per FMA (MIO throttle)

compare.q: Reduction kernel 2 and transposeCoalesced both suffer shared-memory bank conflicts. What access pattern causes each, and what fixes each: padding, or changing which thread reads which word?
answer: transpose: a column read, stride 32 words, fixed by padding the row
reduction kernel 2: index = 2·s·tid, stride 2s words, 2- to 4-way on 32 banks
reduction's fix is sequential addressing (kernel 3), changing which thread reads which word, since the stride changes every step

predict.q: A colleague uses float tile[32][48] to leave room for a wider kernel later. Commit: how many ways does the column read conflict, and what width between 33 and 48 would you pick instead?
predict.answer: 48 mod 32 = 16, so row i starts at bank 16i mod 32, which is only 0 or 16: the 32 lanes share 2 banks, a 16-way conflict (gcd(48, 32) = 16). Any odd width is conflict-free for floats, so 33 (or 49 if they truly need more than 48 columns). Even widths are never fully conflict-free: 34 is 2-way, 36 is 4-way, 40 is 8-way.

apply.task: Run labs/bank-conflicts.py, then add widths 34, 36, 40 and 48 to its layout list. Before running, write the conflict degree you expect for each column read. Then open labs/transpose.ipynb on a T4, run all five kernels, and compute naive → padded and padded ÷ copy for your T4.
apply.done: Your predictions match the lab (34 → 2-way, 36 → 4-way, 40 → 8-way, 48 → 16-way), and you have your T4's five GB/s numbers with both ratios next to Harris's M2050 values (5.29× and 94.6%).
apply.hint: The conflict degree for a float column read is gcd(width, 32). On the T4, expect the naive kernel to lose less than on the M2050 (larger caches), as the K20c already did.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 48-wide conflict, or which width to pick instead?

Were you surprised that coalescing, not bank conflicts, was the bigger step?
